title: The Special Circumstances When Rewards Do Work
hook: A dull checklist can use a bonus; a blank-page problem usually needs a different fuel.
counterintuition: Pink does not abolish rewards. He asks for a stricter match between the incentive and the kind of work in front of you.
tryThisNow: Mark one task as algorithmic or heuristic, then decide whether a reward would support it or distort it.
keyTakeaway: Rewards work best after fair pay is settled, the task is routine, and people receive rationale, respect, and some choice.

breakdown.fastRead: Algorithmic routine tasks are the exception that keeps the argument honest. If the path is clear, the work is not inherently absorbing, and baseline compensation is fair, a reward can help people finish without crowding out much curiosity. Narrow reward fit means using incentives with humility. Baseline compensation comes first, and now-that rewards should feel like appreciation rather than a lever. The rule is to diagnose the task, explain the reason, admit the dullness, and preserve autonomy wherever possible.
breakdown.deepRead: The useful question is not whether a reward exists, but whether it behaves like support or control. Narrow reward fit means Narrow reward fit means matching incentives to tasks where the path is clear, intrinsic interest is low, and the reward does not crowd out creativity. The reward should support completion without pretending to be the whole motivation system. Algorithmic routine tasks: Task type determines whether an incentive is useful or dangerous. Baseline compensation: Money is most effective when it removes money as the main issue. Leaders avoid the false choice between bribing everyone and ignoring compensation. The useful move is to pay fairly, use incentives sparingly, and protect self-direction wherever the work requires care. External rewards are not abolished; they are confined to a smaller and more careful role. Routine work can use rewards when fair baseline pay, rationale, respect, and autonomy keep the incentive from becoming pure control. Carrots and sticks work best for algorithmic tasks and least badly when they are paired with fairness, explanation, and autonomy.
breakdown.fullRead:
The reward exception protects Pink's argument from becoming a slogan. The tempting misread is to preserve old incentive systems by labeling every task routine. The stricter reading requires honest task diagnosis, fair pay before motivational design, and great caution whenever work involves judgment, creativity, learning, or care.

Algorithmic routine tasks: Straightforward work with a known path, such as repetitive processing or simple compliance, does not usually carry deep inner interest. A modest reward can help because there is less spontaneous curiosity to undermine.

Baseline compensation: Wages, benefits, and fairness have to be addressed before appeals to autonomy or purpose can work. People distracted by inequity or insecurity will keep attention on pay because the environment forces them to do so.

Now-that rewards: A surprise reward after good work is less controlling than a promised reward used to steer the work in advance. The reward can register appreciation without turning the task into a bounty hunt.

Adequate baseline rewards must come first because unfair or insufficient pay makes higher motivation difficult to access. Routine tasks have little intrinsic motivation to crowd out, so external rewards can provide a limited motivational boost. A rationale matters because people tolerate dull work better when they understand why it needs doing. Acknowledging boredom preserves respect; pretending a dull task is exciting can make control feel manipulative. Allowing people to choose how to perform routine work adds autonomy even when the task itself is not creative. For nonroutine work, unexpected now-that rewards after completion are less damaging than announced if-then rewards before work begins. Praise works best when it gives information about competence rather than trying to control future behavior.

The critique of carrots and sticks does not erase every incentive. It narrows the zone where incentives make sense and adds guardrails. First, baseline compensation has to be healthy and fair. Without that floor, people naturally obsess over money because insecurity and inequity dominate attention. Second, routine work can accept a reward more safely because the task does not usually contain much intrinsic interest to damage. Even then, three additions matter: explain why the task matters, admit when it is dull, and give people as much choice as possible over how to do it. Those moves keep a necessary incentive from becoming a signal of disrespect. For creative or heuristic work, the safest rewards arrive after the work, not before. A promised if-then prize pulls attention toward the prize while the work is happening. An unexpected now-that reward can feel like recognition, especially when paired with useful feedback about competence. Intangible rewards such as praise follow the same rule: they should inform, not control. The practical result is a restrained incentive toolkit. Pay people enough and fairly enough that money recedes. Use simple rewards for simple tasks. For complex work, favor autonomy, information-rich feedback, and occasional appreciation that does not pre-script effort.

implementationPlan.title: Use incentives only where they fit
